title: Word order and the verb-second rule
theoryMd:
German word order feels chaotic until you learn the one rule that governs it, at which point most of it becomes mechanical. That rule is: **in a main clause, the conjugated verb is the second element.** Not the second *word* — the second *element*.

## Verb-second (V2)

An "element" is one coherent chunk of meaning: a subject, a time expression, a prepositional phrase. Whatever you put first, the conjugated verb follows immediately.

| Position 1 | Verb | Rest |
|---|---|---|
| Ich | **fahre** | morgen nach Berlin. |
| Morgen | **fahre** | ich nach Berlin. |
| Nach Berlin | **fahre** | ich morgen. |
| Mit meinem Bruder | **fahre** | ich morgen nach Berlin. |

Notice what happens in rows 2–4: because something other than the subject took first position, the subject moved to *directly after the verb*. This is called **inversion**, and it is not optional. *Morgen ich fahre…* is simply wrong.

This is the single most common mistake English speakers make, because English allows *Tomorrow I am driving to Berlin* with no reordering.

> Fronting an element is how German emphasises. Putting *Nach Berlin* first says "it's **Berlin** I'm going to". The meaning is the same; the emphasis is not.

## The verb bracket (Satzklammer)

When a sentence has more than one verb part, the conjugated verb stays in position 2 and everything else — infinitive, past participle, separable prefix — goes to the **very end**. The two halves form a bracket around the rest of the sentence.

- *Ich **habe** gestern einen Film **gesehen**.*
- *Ich **will** morgen nach Berlin **fahren**.*
- *Ich **rufe** dich später **an**.*
- *Der Brief **ist** gestern **angekommen**.*

This is why German speakers can hold a listener in suspense: the crucial verb often arrives last. *Ich habe gestern mit meinem Bruder über die Arbeit…* — and only now do you learn whether they *gesprochen*, *gestritten* or *gelacht* have.

With three verb parts, they stack at the end in reverse order: *Ich **werde** morgen nach Berlin **fahren müssen**.*

## Middle field order: TeKaMoLo

Between the two halves of the bracket sits the *Mittelfeld*. Its default order is remembered as **TeKaMoLo**:

- **Te**mporal — *wann?* (when)
- **Ka**usal — *warum?* (why)
- **Mo**dal — *wie?* (how)
- **Lo**kal — *wohin/wo?* (where)

> *Ich fahre **morgen** (Te) **wegen der Arbeit** (Ka) **mit dem Zug** (Mo) **nach Berlin** (Lo).*

This is a default, not a law — you can move an element forward for emphasis. But when in doubt, TeKaMoLo will not sound wrong. One firm rule inside the middle field: **pronouns come early**, right after the verb. *Ich habe **es ihm** gestern gegeben*, not *Ich habe gestern es ihm gegeben*.

## Subordinate clauses: verb last

In a subordinate clause the conjugated verb goes to the **end**. Subordinating conjunctions that trigger this include *dass, weil, wenn, ob, als, obwohl, damit, bevor, nachdem, während, seit*, and all relative pronouns.

- *Ich weiß, **dass** er morgen nach Berlin **fährt**.*
- *Ich bleibe zu Hause, **weil** ich krank **bin**.*
- *Wir gehen spazieren, **wenn** das Wetter schön **ist**.*

If the clause has a verb bracket, the conjugated verb goes right to the end, *after* the participle or infinitive — the bracket collapses:

- *…, weil ich den Film **gesehen habe**.* (not *habe gesehen*)
- *…, weil ich nach Berlin **fahren will**.*

And if a subordinate clause comes **first**, the whole clause counts as element number one — so the main clause verb follows immediately:

> ***Weil ich krank bin**, **bleibe** ich zu Hause.*

You get two verbs meeting in the middle, separated by a comma. That collision is a good sign you have built the sentence correctly.

## The conjunctions that change nothing

Five coordinating conjunctions simply join two main clauses and do **not** affect word order at all. Remember them as **ADUSO**:

*aber, denn, und, sondern, oder*

- *Ich bleibe zu Hause, **denn** ich **bin** krank.* (verb second — normal)
- *Ich bleibe zu Hause, **weil** ich krank **bin**.* (verb last — subordinate)

*Denn* and *weil* mean much the same thing but behave completely differently. If you can only remember one pair, remember this one.

## Questions and commands

- **Yes/no question:** verb takes first position. ***Fährst** du morgen nach Berlin?*
- **W-question:** the question word is element one, verb second. ***Wann fährst** du nach Berlin?*
- **Imperative:** verb first. ***Fahr** nach Berlin!*

payload.explanation: Subject first, conjugated verb second, then time before place.
When a time expression takes first position, the subject must move behind the verb — inversion.
The conjugated verb must be the second element, so after 'Morgen' comes 'fahre', then the subject.

payload.prompt: gesehen / ich / einen Film / habe / gestern
answers: Ich habe gestern einen Film gesehen
payload.explanation: The verb bracket: 'habe' second, past participle 'gesehen' at the very end.
The separable prefix moves to the end of the main clause, closing the verb bracket.
'weil' is subordinating, so the conjugated verb goes to the very end of the clause.

payload.prompt: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank ___ .
payload.explanation: Subordinate clause with weil → the conjugated verb 'bin' comes last.

payload.prompt: Which conjunction does NOT send the verb to the end?
payload.explanation: denn is coordinating (ADUSO: aber, denn, und, sondern, oder) and leaves word order untouched. weil, dass and obwohl are subordinating.

payload.prompt: bleibe / weil ich krank bin / ich / zu Hause
answers: Weil ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause
payload.explanation: A subordinate clause in first position counts as element one, so the main verb 'bleibe' follows immediately after the comma.
In a subordinate clause the conjugated verb goes right to the end, after the participle: gesehen habe.

payload.prompt: mit dem Zug / ich / nach Berlin / fahre / morgen
answers: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin
payload.explanation: Middle field default: temporal (morgen), then modal (mit dem Zug), then local (nach Berlin).

payload.prompt: Turn 'Du fährst morgen nach Berlin.' into a yes/no question.
payload.explanation: In a yes/no question the conjugated verb moves to first position, subject immediately after.
